summary: Every dry season, fires burn Borneo's forests and peatlands, and the smoke hides them from the satellites that take ordinary photos. Borneo Through the Smoke is an interactive web map that uses NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar, which sees through smoke and cloud, to track where tree cover disappeared across Indonesian Borneo from June to October 2026, 12 days at a time. Radar's cross-polarized (HV) echo comes from leaves and branches, so when canopy burns, that echo collapses. The app tells the season as a four-chapter story: the smoke and fire gas that reached Singapore and Kuala Lumpur, the 3,021 km² of tree cover the radar flagged as lost, an independent check against NASA fire detections (4 times more than chance) and NASA's optical change map (6 times), and the cost: an estimated 22 to 28 million tonnes of CO₂ from burning peat. It shows what NISAR makes possible: forest-loss maps during a fire season, not months after the smoke clears.
details:
What it does. Borneo Through the Smoke is an interactive map that tells Borneo's 2026 fire season in four steps: the smoke and fire gas that hid it from ordinary satellites; the 3,021 km² of tree cover that NASA-ISRO's NISAR radar saw disappear through that smoke; proof from NASA's fire and optical satellites, which match the radar 4 to 6 times more often than chance; and the cost, an estimated 22 to 28 million tonnes of CO₂ from burning peat.

How it works. A Python pipeline turns 612 NISAR radar images into a loss map every 12 days. When forest burns, the radar's cross-polarized echo (HV), which bounces off leaves and branches, collapses, while the ground echo (HH) changes less. We checked the result against NASA FIRMS, OPERA, VIIRS and AIRS data and the Peat-ML peat map. The radar values come from preview images and the CO₂ figure is an estimate, so the app says both.

Benefits and impact. Optical satellites go blind in the fire season, exactly when it matters. With radar, fire and forestry agencies could see forest loss within 12 days instead of months later; carbon accounting gets a measured area for peat fires, among the largest and least-measured emission sources; and dated maps help hold illegal land clearing to account. We want NISAR's free data to become a fire-season tool anyone can open in a browser, for any region where smoke or cloud blocks the view.

Built with Python (NumPy, SciPy), JavaScript with Leaflet, HTML and CSS, hosted free on GitHub Pages. No special hardware: team laptops. Code written with Claude Code (Anthropic) under the team's direction. Open source (Apache-2.0); full method and limits in the README.
